content: Cullin-5 is a protein encoded by the CUL5 gene in humans. The mammalian product of this gene was initially identified through expression cloning because of its ability to mobilize intracellular calcium in response to the peptide hormone arginine vasopressin. At the time of its discovery, it was named VACM-1, which stands for vasopressin-activated, calcium-mobilizing receptor. Subsequent research revealed that VACM-1 is homologous to the Cullin family of proteins, leading to its renaming as Cullin-5 (CUL5). The expression of the CUL5 protein is most prominent in heart and skeletal muscle tissues. It is also specifically expressed in the vascular endothelium and the renal collecting tubules. CUL5 plays a role in inhibiting cellular proliferation. This function is thought to be mediated through its involvement in the SOCS/BC-box/eloBC/CUL5/RING E3 ligase complex, which is a component of the ubiquitin-proteasome system responsible for targeted protein degradation. Additionally, one study has demonstrated that CUL5 is involved in the Reelin signaling cascade. It contributes to the degradation of DAB1, thereby maintaining the negative feedback mechanism of Reelin signaling during corticogenesis. CUL5 has been shown to interact with RBX1, a key component of the ubiquitin ligase complex.
